claims.text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is a single-phase FCC alloy after casting and homogenization.
CoCrFeMnNi can retain its single-phase character after recrystallization or severe plastic deformation.
Controlled elemental substitution can increase atomic size mismatch in CoCrFeMnNi.
Increasing atomic size mismatch increases local lattice distortion.
Increased atomic size mismatch creates local strain fields and lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions obstruct dislocation motion.
Elevated resistance to dislocation motion governs alloy strength in a concentrated FCC alloy.
Increasing local lattice distortion increases yield strength in CoCrFeMnNi.
Increasing local lattice distortion increases hardness in CoCrFeMnNi.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can quantify local lattice distortion in these samples.
Atom probe tomography can quantify local atomic size mismatch or local lattice distortion.
XRD, electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography can provide evidence that CoCrFeMnNi remains single phase.
The baseline Cantor alloy has minimal atomic size mismatch and lower lattice distortion.
The baseline Cantor alloy has lower hardness and yield strength than size-mismatch-increased substituted samples.
Substituted samples with greater XRD peak broadening and APT-indicated local distortion will have higher hardness and yield strength than the baseline.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys that do not develop secondary phases or major phase-stability changes.
Elemental substitution may also alter bonding characteristics or promote minor phase segregation that affects mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes elemental substitution while also requiring elemental concentrations to remain constant. Replacing one element with another necessarily changes at least those elements' concentrations unless a specific coupled-composition scheme is defined.

The boundary places samples containing secondary phases outside the hypothesis's intended domain, whereas the falsification rule treats detection of secondary phases as evidence that falsifies the hypothesis rather than as a failed scope condition.
